the choice of spike sorting algorithm has a significant impact on the results of spike train analysis.
the Valley-Seeking algorithm is the best choice for spike sorting of extracellular recordings of human subthalamic nucleus.

spike sorting algorithms produce different results, that the choice of the sorting method is crucial for the analysis, and that the best algorithm for a specific data set can only be determined by a validation procedure based on ground truth.

the analysis of spike train data obtained in Parkinson's disease patients.
the analysis of spike train synchrony and the evaluation of spike sorting algorithms.
the development of a standardized procedure to evaluate the quality of spike sorting algorithms.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is no single best algorithm.
there is not one best spike-sorting algorithm.
the Valley-Seeking algorithm produces the best results in our data, but that this is only the best of a very bad lot.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
spike sorting is a difficult and error-prone procedure, which should be performed with care.
the Valley-Seeking algorithm is a good choice for sorting extracellular data.
the K-Meanness algorithm is the best choice in the presence of a high number of artifacts.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is important to use spike sorting validation procedures to ensure that spike sorting results are reliable.
the spike sorting problem cannot be solved by a unique algorithm.
spike sorting is a crucial step in the analysis of spike data, and that the algorithm used to do this step is of paramount importance for the subsequent analysis.
